To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the synthetic penta‐acyl lipid As from P. gingivialis, as well as tri‐acyl lipid A, are able to stimulate macrophages and monocytes via TLR4.
compound PG‐381– 5FA, a chemically synthesized lipid A from P. gingivitis, activates immune cells via TLR4, and is a potent agonist for IL‐6 production in human peripheral blood monocyte cells.

compound PG‐381– 5FA, a synthetic lipid A derived from P.gingivalis strain 382 possessing a penta‐fattyl acyl chains, induces the expression of inflammatory mediators in a manner dependent on TLR4/mD‐ 2, similar to that observed with compound 506, a synthetic lipidA derived from E.coli.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the lipid A species of P. gingival is recognized by the innate immune system through TLR4‐mediated signal pathways.
the lipid A portion of P. gingival is recognized by TLR4 in a manner similar, but not identical, to that of E. coli‐type lipid A.

compound 506, compound PG‐3FA and compound PG‐5FA are all agonists for TLR4, but compound PG‐5FAs are much stronger agonist than compound PG‐3FAs, and that compound PG‐5Fa is a stronger agonist than E. coli‐type compound 506.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the chemical synthesis, using a penta‐fused pyridine as an important intermediate, of a lipid A possessing the penta‐acyl chains of the lipid A of P. gingivalisis a useful tool for understanding the biological activities of the lipid A.
the penta‐acyl chain lipid A from P. gingi valis can be a useful tool for studying the role of TLR4 in the immune response.
compound PG‐381–FA, which is a lipid A from P. gingivitis, can be used as a tool to study TLR4‐mediated innate immunity.
